role: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, project sponsor and EIS preparer
stance_basis: HUD authored the EIS, prepared responses defending the project's analysis, and explicitly rebutted DOT objections to justify including the Downtown Expressway as a relevant environmental consideration
summary: HUD is the project sponsor and EIS preparer for the Randolph Urban Renewal Project, and in this chapter it responds to comments from other agencies. HUD defends its methodology, particularly its decision to analyze the Downtown Expressway's impacts on the project area, citing NEPA requirements and EPA confirmation. HUD also addresses requests for additional air quality data, traffic documentation, and noise analysis clarifications, explaining constraints while maintaining the validity of its assessments.
complaint_summary: HUD defends its assessment that the Downtown Expressway will have a significant negative environmental impact on Randolph, citing detailed noise studies, air quality findings, and traffic data, and reaffirming that these impacts required investigation under NEPA.

statement.text:
The largest, single problem that affects the Randolph project is the traffic noise that will be generated by the Downtown Expressway. The Draft Statement documented in detail the noise impacts based on a study done by one of the leading acoustical consulting firms in the country. HUD standards for acceptable exterior noise level in residential areas appears on page 19 of the statement. Figure No. 7 maps out the areas in Randolph that will be so impacted by noise that they will fall into the "normally unacceptable" category. The "normally unacceptable" zone is defined in HUD's Noise Assessment Guidelines handbooks as an area where the noise exposure is severe to the degree that unusual and costly building constructions are necessary to ensure some tranquility indoors, and barriers must be erected between the site and prominent noise sources to make the outdoor environment tolerable. Because the affected areas are located in primarily residential areas, it is obvious that left untreated this problem would constitute a significant negative environment impact on Randolph.
In addition to this problem, the Draft Statement also discussed the potential impacts of increased air pollution and intense spill light from the expressway lighting. Nowhere in the discussion on these two issues stated definitively that these impacts would make any area of Randolph unacceptable. The conclusion of the lighting paragraph was that "the lighting of the Downtown Expressway could have a detrimental effect." The finding on the issue of air quality was somewhat stronger "the impact on air quality caused chiefly by vehicular traffic is likely to be negative because of the large numbers of automobiles and trucks moving through the Randolph Area on the Downtown Expressway." The discussion on comparative traffic counts in response to Question 2 of the Department of Transportation's comments and on air quality in response to Question 1 of the Environmental Protection Agency bears out this assessment. It was necessary to investigate these two problems as probable effects of a segment of a major Expressway in a highly urban area.

statement.closing_anchor: It was necessary to investigate these two problems as probable effects of a segment of a major Expressway in a highly urban area.
